 1   Q   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 2   A   Matthew P. Smith. My business address is 16690 Swingley Ridge Road,

 3       Suite 140, Chesterfield, MO 63017.



 4   Q   WHAT IS YOUR OCCUPATION?

 5   A   I am a consultant in the field of public utility regulation and a Senior

 6       Consultant with the firm of Brubaker & Associates, Inc. (“BAI”), energy,

 7       economic and regulatory consultants.



 8   Q   PLEASE        DESCRIBE          YOUR         EDUCATIONAL          AND

 9       PROFESSIONAL BACKGROUND.

10   A   This information is included as Appendix A to my testimony.



11   Q   ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU APPEARING IN THIS

12       PROCEEDING?

13   A   I am appearing on behalf of the Federal Executive Agencies (“FEA”) and

14       Louisiana Energy Services L.L.C. d/b/a URENCO USA (“LES”). FEA and

15       LES own and operate facilities in the Southwestern Public Service

16       Company (“SPS” or “Company”) service territory.




                                      Page 1
                           Direct Testimony of Matthew P. Smith
                            NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


1    Q   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY IN THIS

2        PROCEEDING?

3    A   The purpose of my testimony is to address the reasonableness of SPS’s

4        proposed retail Class Cost of Service Study (“CCOSS”) and its proposed

5        spread of the approved revenue increase across rate classes.

6               My silence with regard to any position taken by SPS in its

7        application or direct testimony in this proceeding does not indicate my

8        endorsement of that position.



 9               I. Summary of Findings and Recommendations

10   Q   PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR RECOMMENDATIONS AND

11       FINDINGS.

12   A   In my testimony, I recommend the following:

13          SPS’s CCOSS study be adjusted to allocate all production resources on
14           the Company’s Average and Excess 4-Coincident Peak Demand (“AED
15           4-CP”) production allocator. The Company’s proposed allocation of
16           some renewable production resources, such as the Hale and Sagamore
17           wind facilities, on an energy basis is inappropriate as these resources are
18           utilized within the SPS production resource portfolio to provide reliable
19           firm service at reasonable energy costs. The renewable resource does
20           provide accredited resource capacity to satisfy SPS’s resource adequacy
21           obligations and permit it to reliably serve its customers’ peak demands.

22          SPS’s revenue allocation, or spread, is inappropriate. The Company
23           uses total revenue, rather than base rate revenues, to allocate the revenue
24           increases calculated by the CCOSS. This creates a mismatch between
25           the costs which are being assigned through the CCOSS, which are base

                                         Page 2
                          Direct Testimony of Matthew P. Smith
                           NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1          rate revenues, and the revenue allocation method used by the Company,
 2          which uses total revenue to spread costs from the CCOSS to customer
 3          classes. To rectify the distorted revenue spread, the revenue allocation
 4          should be based on base rate revenues only.



 5                    II. SPS’s Class Cost of Service Study

 6   Q   PLEASE DESCRIBE THE COMPANY'S PROPOSED CCOSS IN

 7       THIS CASE.

 8   A   Company witness Taylor Hurt sponsored the Company’s CCOSS. As

 9       discussed in Mr. Hurt’s testimony at pages 14-38, he outlines the

10       Company’s CCOSS to include the following:

11       1. Functionalize costs between production, transmission, distribution and
12          customer service components.

13       2. Classify the functionalized costs between:

14          i. Demand, or fixed costs that are incurred to provide reliable service
15             and which are properly reflected as capacity charges or allocations;

16          ii. Energy, or costs that vary based on hourly demands and are costs
17              typically reflected as energy (in kWh) charges; and

18          iii. Customer components, or fixed costs that reflect customer-related
19               connections, accounts and servicing costs.

20       Mr. Hurt outlined classification of his functionalized costs in his Table

21       TJH-1 at page 18 of his testimony, which I have copied below as Table

22       MPS-1.

1   Q     DID MR. HURT HAVE ANY EXCEPTIONS TO HIS ALLOCATION

2         OF FUNCTIONALIZED PRODUCTION DEMAND COSTS?

3   A     Yes. Mr. Hurt proposes to classify production wind related assets, such as

4         the Sagamore and Hale wind generation resources, as energy costs rather

5         than as demand costs as he has done for all other SPS generating resources.


                                           Page 4
                              Direct Testimony of Matthew P. Smith
                               NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


1    Q   WHY IS SPS PROPOSING TO CLASSIFY THESE RENEWABLE

2        RESOURCES AS ENERGY AND ALLOCATE THEM ACROSS

3        CLASSES BASED ON ENERGY CONSUMPTION?

4    A   Mr. Hurt provided no basis for this allocation of production resources on

5        energy, rather than demand, other than the fact that the Company has

6        provided a cost-based justification for functionalizing and allocating

 7       resources that are included within the SPS production resource portfolio

 8       differently than the other assets included in its resource portfolio. He does

 9       state that SPS has made this functionalization proposal for certain

10       renewable resources in the past, but again provides no support for the

11       reasonableness of this recommendation in this case.1



12   Q   DO YOU AGREE WITH MR. HURT THAT THE HALE AND

13       SAGAMORE              PRODUCTION            RESOURCES            SHOULD   BE

14       CLASSIFIED AS ENERGY, RATHER THAN DEMAND, WHICH IS

15       INCONSISTENT             WITH      ALL      OTHER          SPS   PRODUCTION

16       RESOURCES?

17   A   No, I disagree for several reasons.          First, renewable resources have

18       accredited capacity toward SPS’s planning reserve margin, making these



         1
             Direct Testimony of SPS Witness Taylor Hurt, page 25.

                                            Page 5
                          Direct Testimony of Matthew P. Smith
                           NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1       units capacity resources that are relied on by SPS to meet its resource

 2       capacity obligations to provide service to its “Firm Load Obligations.”

 3              Hence, these resources provide system benefits for both adding

 4       capacity needed to service the peak hour and peak critical hour demands on

 5       the system, as well as to service the base hourly energy system demands.

 6       Also, because renewable resources do not have a fuel cost associated with

 7       energy output, the Hale and Sagamore resources’ annual costs are largely

 8       fixed and do not vary with the energy output of the resources. Therefore,

 9       allocating these costs across rate classes based on this fixed cost is

10       consistent with how all other fixed production resource costs are allocated

11       across jurisdictions and New Mexico rate classes.



12   Q   HAS SPS ALLOCATED THESE RESOURCES AS ENERGY IN

13       PAST CASES?

14   A   Yes, but that allocation was based on a settlement that limited the use of an

15       energy allocation to the first-rate case after the resources were placed

16       in-service, and the settlement then specified that the classification and

17       allocation would be revisited in subsequent rate cases.

18              Specifically, in the Stipulation in the Hale/Sagamore CCN case,

19       Case No. 17-00044-UT, the Commission approved allocating these costs on



                                        Page 6
                               Direct Testimony of Matthew P. Smith
                                NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


1           a jurisdictional basis using an energy allocator for the first-rate case after

2           each resource was placed in service. The Stipulation clearly stated that this

3           allocation would not hold for subsequent SPS rate cases. The Company’s

4           resource mix has changed since the date of the CCN settlement approval2

 5          and SPS’s last rate case in 2023.3

 6                  The Stipulation in the Hale CCN proceeding, Case No.

 7          17-00044-UT, prescribes an energy allocation between the Texas, New

 8          Mexico, and wholesale jurisdictions but also states that “[t]he Commission

 9          can change this allocation method in future proceedings based upon the

10          facts at that time.”4

11                  The Stipulation clearly contemplated that, to the extent Hale and

12          Sagamore will eventually provide both capacity and energy benefits to the

13          system, the costs should be allocated in accordance with the benefits these

14          resources provide to the system, as provided in Stipulation paragraph X,

15          Jurisdictional Allocation:

16                  This provision applies to both the Hale and Sagamore
17                  projects. In New Mexico retail cases, the project costs will
18                  be allocated among SPS rate jurisdictions based upon an
19                  energy allocator.   The Commission can change this



            2
               Final Order Adopting Certification of Stipulation with Modification (March 21,
     2018), Case No. 17-00044-UT.
             3
               Case No. 22-00286-UT.
             4
               Unanimous Comprehensive Stipulation, at 15, Case No. 17-00044-UT.

                                             Page 7

                                NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1                  allocation method in future proceedings based upon the facts
 2                  at that time.

 3          The Final Order Adopting that Stipulation is dated March 21, 2018.

 4                  A continued allocation of energy does not accurately reflect the

 5          benefits that these resources provide to SPS customers. Therefore, an

 6          energy allocation does not fairly and reasonably allocate these resources to

 7          customer classes that align with the benefits received by rate classes. The

 8          accredited capacity from these renewable resources is needed by SPS to

 9          comply with its resource adequacy requirement imposed by the Southwest

10          Power Pool (“SPP”).5 As seen on my Attachment MPS-2, which I discuss

11          in more detail later, these renewable resources do provide SPS customer

12          resource capacity that is needed to provide reliable firm service to its rate

13          classes.   Hence, like all resources in SPS's production portfolio, its

14          renewable resources provide both the capacity to serve average demands

15          and its excess demand throughout the year. For this reason, the most

16          accurate and fair classification for all SPS production resources is

17          production capacity and these capacity resources are allocated using a A&E

18          4CP, which develops a production allocator to allocate the production




            5
              See Attachment MPS-2, Summary of SPS Planning Forecast (2024-2033) L&R
     Table. The table shows SPS’s accredited capacity for each year, compared to SPS’s firm
     load obligation and planning reserve margin.

                                            Page 8
                          Direct Testimony of Matthew P. Smith
                           NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1       resource portfolio cost across rate bases based on the operation of the

 2       portfolio to serve both average demands, and excess demands.

 3              Finally, with the continued retirement of coal-fired generating

 4       resources, which is having a significant impact on SPS's capacity planning

 5       reserve margin, these wind resources will be needed for capacity adequacy.

 6       Retirement of coal-fired resources is enhancing the value and importance of

 7       the capacity provided by Hale and Sagamore, which is needed for SPS to

 8       meet its resource capacity obligations.

 9              For all these reasons, the Hale and Sagamore facilities should be

10       allocated in a manner that reasonably reflects the benefits these resources

11       provide to SPS and its ability to provide reliable peak day and average

12       annual energy service to its customers.



13   Q   DO THE SAGAMORE AND HALE FACILITIES PROVIDE

14       ACCREDITED CAPACITY NECESSARY TO MEET SPS’S PEAK

15       LOAD OBLIGATIONS, AND TO SATISFY ITS SOUTHWEST

16       POWER POOL INTEGRATED PLANNING RESERVE MARGIN

17       REQUIREMENTS?

18   A   Yes. A comparison of SPS’s own generation resources, along with their

19       nameplate rating and accredited capacity used to meet the SPS planning



                                        Page 9
                              Direct Testimony of Matthew P. Smith
                               NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


1           reserve margin, are outlined on my Attachment MPS-1. As shown on this

2           attachment, for calendar year 2027, the Hale (74 MW) and Sagamore

3           (81 MW) accredited capacity is approximately 155 MW, and this accredited

4           capacity is projected to remain steady over time, including the period in

5           which rates adopted in this proceeding will be in effect.6

6                  On my Attachment MPS-2, I show the resource adequacy projection

7           SPS included in its 2023 Integrated Resource Plan (“IRP”). The table is on

8           page 88 of the 2023 IRP. As shown on my attachment, SPS does include

 9          owned renewables as capacity resources available to meet its peak load plus

10          the SPS prescribed 15% minimum planning reserve margin. Further, on

11          this attachment, SPS’s owned renewable resources, which include Hale and

12          Sagamore, provide approximately 500 MW of capacity, in 2027, to meet

13          SPS’s resource requirements. As outlined in its IRP presentation, SPS

14          included its owned renewable resources for its Load and Resource Planning

15          Forecast.   Those owned renewable resources make strong capacity

16          contributions to its resource capacity obligations, and are needed in order

17          for SPS to meet its customers’ demand every hour of the year, including

18          peak hour, and critical peak period hours.       As such, these renewable




            6
             On Attachment MPS-1, page 2, I recreated the Company’s response to SPS-OPL
     1-22 (Exhibit SPS-OPL 1-23, tab L&R).

                                           Page 10
                          Direct Testimony of Matthew P. Smith
                           NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1       resources do make capacity contributions as well as energy contributions to

 2       the system.



 3   Q   HOW DID MR. HURT DEVELOP PRODUCTION DEMAND

 4       ALLOCATION FACTORS FOR USE IN HIS CCOSS?

 5   A   For the allocation of fixed production and transmission investments, Mr.

 6       Hurt proposes an A&E 4CP allocation methodology. This methodology

 7       provides consideration to average demand (or average hourly energy

 8       consumption), and hourly demands in excess of average hourly demands.

 9       The capacity available to serve the excess of average hourly demands

10       represents the capacity needed to serve peak hour and critical hour demands.

11       The A&E 4CP methodology weights the average demand by Mr. Hurt's

12       calculation of system load factor, and weights the excess demands by 1

13       minus the load factor. The A&E 4CP is the weighted average of system

14       average demand and excess hour demands. Mr. Hurt calculates system load

15       factor using a 4CP peak methodology.



16   Q   HOW DID MR. HURT DEVELOP TRANSMISSION CAPACITY

17       COST ALLOCATORS?

18   A   Similar to production, Mr. Hurt relied on an A&E 4CP.



                                       Page 11
                          Direct Testimony of Matthew P. Smith
                           NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1   Q   HOW DID MR. HURT DEVELOP DISTRIBUTION COST

 2       ALLOCATORS?

 3   A   Mr. Hurt allocates distribution plant investment on a non-coincident peak

 4       (“NCP”) basis. He states the NCP, as opposed to a coincident peak, is

 5       appropriate for distribution plant because this plant is sized to meet

 6       localized demand to provide service to customer classes that are similar in

 7       size and demands.



 8   Q   WHAT DO YOU RECOMMEND?

 9   A   I recommend the Commission reject SPS’s proposed CCOSS and approve

10       a CCOSS based on SPS's study, but adjusted to classify and allocate all

11       production resource portfolio fixed costs as demand and allocate these costs

12       using the production capacity allocation factor.

1   Q            ARE THERE CHANGES IN CIRCUMSTANCES THAT THE

2                COMMISSION SHOULD CONSIDER IN DETERMINING THE

3                JURISDICTIONAL                      ALLOCATION               OF          THE     HALE          AND

4                SAGAMORE GENERATION RESOURCES?

5   A            Yes. These resources have become necessary for SPS to meet its resource

6                adequacy requirement imposed by the SPP, which, for the summer, was

7                recently increased from 15% to 16%, with a 15% Planning Reserve Margin

8                (“PRM”) established for the winter in 2025/2026 which will escalate to 36%




                                                             Page 13
                              Direct Testimony of Matthew P. Smith
                               NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1       in 2026/2027, as discussed in SPS witness Gable’s testimony.7 Further, as

 2       more of SPS’s coal-fired generating resources are retired, the accredited

 3       capacity of these resources will become more meaningful to SPS to meet its

 4       capacity resource adequacy requirement set by the SPP. This will continue

 5       to grow over time, as SPS relies more on renewable non-carbon emitting

 6       resources as part of its production infrastructure needed to meet the capacity

 7       demands and energy requirements of its customers.



 8                               III. Revenue Allocation

 9   Q   HOW DOES SPS PROPOSE TO ALLOCATE ITS REQUESTED

10       REVENUE INCREASE AMONG THE NEW MEXICO RETAIL

11       RATE CLASSES?

12   A   SPS’s proposed spread of the revenue deficiency, performed by

13       Mr. Trowbridge, follows the results of its CCOSS, but it works toward a

14       gradual movement to cost of service in this case by limiting increases to any

15       specific rate class to 1.5x the system average increase, setting a minimum

16       increase for classes priced above cost of service to 1.0x the system average

17       increase. However, when applying the above maximum and minimum

18       increases, Mr. Trowbridge does so in accordance with the total revenue,



         7
             Direct Testimony of SPS Witness Justin Gable, pages 19 & 20.

                                           Page 14
                          Direct Testimony of Matthew P. Smith
                           NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1       which is base rate revenue plus fuel and purchased power costs, renewable

 2       portfolio standard costs, energy efficiency costs, electric vehicle

 3       infrastructure costs, and grid modernization costs – rather than setting the

 4       limits based on base rate revenue.



 5   Q   IS   APPLYING       MR.     TROWBRIDGE’S           REVENUE       SPREAD

 6       METHODOLOGY TO TOTAL REVENUES APPROPRIATE? IF

 7       NOT, PLEASE EXPLAIN.

8    A   While I agree with the principles of gradualism, applying Mr. Trowbridge’s

9        revenue spread methodology to total revenue, instead of base rate revenue,

10       is not appropriate. The revenue spread process begins with the output from

11       the CCOSS results, which allocates, or assigns, base rate revenue costs to

12       customer classes.    The CCOSS does not assign costs based on total

13       revenues.     Including the additional categories of costs which

14       Mr. Trowbridge has erroneously used as the basis for his revenue spread

15       methodology, therefore, is not appropriate.

16              By using total revenue as the starting point of his revenue spread,

17       Mr. Trowbridge has diluted the results of the CCOSS. This dilution can be

18       observed by comparing the system average increase of 16.7%, when

19       viewing the proposed increase through the lens of total revenue, compared



                                       Page 15
                           Direct Testimony of Matthew P. Smith
                            NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


1        to the actual system average increase of 24.4% on a base rates revenue basis,

2        which the CCOSS produces. The actual total increase to customer class

3        revenue, however, remains the same despite the framing of the system

4        average increase. But the allocation, or spread, of revenues to classes is

 5       skewed when using Mr. Trowbridge’s method, due to the discontinuity

 6       between the costs being allocated in the CCOSS and the final allocation of

 7       said costs by Mr. Trowbridge’s revenue spread.



 8   Q   IS SPS’S PROPOSED REVENUE SPREAD REASONABLE IN THIS

 9       CASE?

10   A   No. Because SPS’s CCOSS is flawed, Mr. Trowbridge’s revenue allocation

11       starts with an inaccurate model. Further, the improper inclusion of cost

12       categories outside of the CCOSS, which formulate the total revenues, drives

13       the revenue spread farther still from actual cost causation. Hence, I propose

14       a revenue spread that reflects my corrected CCOSS and revenue spread

15       methodology. To align with the CCOSS, under my methodology revenue

16       is spread to customer classes using base rate revenues. I recommend

17       limiting classes to increases of no more than 1.5x the system average

18       increase of 24.4%, and no less than 0.5x the system average increase. This

19       method preserves the cost causation principles from the CCOSS, assigning

1         revenue responsibility to each customer class, while also applying

2         gradualism to the revenue spread. My proposed class revenue spread, using
